title: LGL Ltd. v. R (1999 TCC) Tax Court of Canada Decision
subject: TCC trial decision on whether field data collection performed outside Canada qualified for SR&ED investment tax credits.
outcome: Appeal dismissed; foreign field work fell under s. 37(2), not s. 37(1)(a), and earned no ITCs (affirmed by the FCA in 2000).
keyPhrase: LGL Ltd v The Queen 1999 TCC
summary: LGL Ltd. v. The Queen (1999 TCC) is a Tax Court of Canada ruling for SR&ED claimants holding that field data collection physically performed outside Canada falls under subsection 37(2), not paragraph 37(1)(a), even when scientifically indispensable. For 1991–1993, foreign field costs and allocable overhead earned no investment tax credit; only work carried on in Canada qualified.
metaDescription: Examine the 1999 Tax Court of Canada ruling in LGL Ltd. v. R (The Queen) regarding Canadian SR&ED tax credit expenditures.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background
Corporate Profile and Operational Context

The landmark decision of the Tax Court of Canada in LGL Ltd. v. R. (formal style of cause LGL Limited v. Her Majesty The Queen, Docket 96-4726(IT)G, reported at [1999] 2 C.T.C. 2482 and 99 D.T.C. 675) stands as a foundational authority governing the territorial boundaries of Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentives in Canada. Heard on November 23 and 24, 1998, with judgment delivered on January 12, 1999, by Judge Donald G.H. Bowman (Bowman T.C.J.), the case addressed whether physical data-collection activities performed outside Canadian borders as an indispensable component of a Canadian-directed research project could qualify as SR&ED "carried on in Canada".

The appellant, LGL Limited, was a Canadian-incorporated environmental research firm owned and managed by Canadians. The corporation had offices and laboratories in King City, Ontario; Sidney, British Columbia; and St. John's, Newfoundland, and was also affiliated with two research companies in Texas and Alaska. LGL Limited's core scientific mandate encompassed advanced ecological and biological investigations across terrestrial, freshwater, and marine ecosystems, alongside specialized aviation safety studies analyzing bird hazards to aircraft. Specifically, the four projects under review (the Whale, Oldsquaw, Eider, and Endicott Fish Projects) related broadly to the environmental effects of offshore and coastal oil and gas exploration and development on whales, birds, and fish. Because the data forming the basis of the research had to be collected off the northern coast of Alaska—where, depending on the project, the only location in which the whales could safely be observed (off Point Barrow), previously disturbed and undisturbed moulting areas with nine years of background survey data, or the oil-industry causeways under study (none of which exist in the Canadian Arctic) were located—the appellant's Canadian researchers and personnel had to carry out the field data collection outside Canada. Once acquired, these field datasets were brought back to LGL Limited's Canadian laboratories, where scientists assimilated, modeled, and analyzed the data to complete the scientific studies.
The Taxpayer's Claim and the Crown's Challenge

In filing its corporate income tax returns for the 1991, 1992, and 1993 taxation years, LGL Limited claimed that the entirety of its project costs—including direct salaries, travel expenses, field outlays, and the corresponding allocation of corporate overhead attributable to time and money spent outside Canada—qualified as current expenditures on SR&ED "carried on in Canada" pursuant to paragraph 37(1)(a) of the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148, as amended (the "Act"). By classifying the foreign field data collection under subsection 37(1), the appellant sought to include both the direct foreign field costs and their associated overhead allocations in its pool of qualified SR&ED expenditures, thereby generating refundable Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) under section 127 of the Act.

The Minister of National Revenue assessed LGL Limited for the 1991, 1992, and 1993 taxation years, denying the subsection 37(1) treatment and the corresponding refundable ITCs for the portion of time and money expended outside Canada. The Crown (represented at trial by counsel Alexandra K. Brown and Sanjana Bhatia, opposing appellant's counsel Russell D. Laishley) conceded a critical threshold point: the Respondent admitted that each of the disputed environmental projects, when viewed in its entirety, met the scientific and technological criteria to qualify as eligible SR&ED under section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations (the "Regulations"). However, the Crown maintained that the physical location where the work was executed governed its statutory classification under section 37. Consequently, the Crown asserted that expenditures for data collection physically performed outside Canada could only be deducted under subsection 37(2) as research "carried on outside Canada," a provision under which, as the Court noted, current expenditures on SR&ED carried on outside Canada do not give rise to an ITC; the portion of overhead allocable to that work, which formed part of the appellant's claim, would likewise fall outside paragraph 37(1)(a).

A secondary evidentiary dispute initially arose regarding two specific undertakings—the Snow Goose Project and the Eider Project—in respect of which the question was whether they were projects of the Canadian appellant or of LGL Alaska, one of the two research companies (in Texas and Alaska) with which LGL Limited was affiliated. The parties resolved this entity-attribution dispute by filing a partial consent to judgment agreeing that both the Snow Goose Project and the Eider Project were indeed projects of LGL Limited and not of LGL Alaska; the Court found it unnecessary to set out the detailed terms of the consent.
Governing Statutory Framework

The legal architecture governing the dispute during the 1991, 1992, and 1993 taxation years rested on the interplay between section 37, section 127, and Regulation 2900. Under paragraph 37(1)(a) of the Act, a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada could deduct current expenditures made in the year or in a preceding taxation year ending after 1973 "on scientific research and experimental development carried on in Canada, directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer, and related to a business of the taxpayer". Expenditures meeting the requirements of subsection 37(1) could be carried forward indefinitely in a cumulative SR&ED expenditure pool, could include the allowable overhead allocable to the SR&ED (in LGL Limited's case, computed under a formula that the parties agreed was acceptable), and entitled the taxpayer to an ITC under section 127, giving rise to a credit against tax otherwise payable or a refund to the extent the taxpayer was unable to utilize the credit.

Conversely, subsection 37(2) of the Act governed current expenditures made by a taxpayer "on scientific research and experimental development carried on outside Canada, directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer, and related to a business of the taxpayer". While subsection 37(2) permitted an immediate deduction in computing business income for the year in which the foreign research expenditure was incurred, such amounts could not be pooled and carried forward in the manner available under subsection 37(1) and, as the Court expressly noted, did not give rise to an ITC. Finally, during the years in issue, paragraph 37(7) of the Act stipulated that "scientific research and experimental development" had the meaning assigned by regulation, directing the statutory inquiry to Regulation 2900. Under Regulation 2900(1), SR&ED was defined as a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis—comprising basic research, applied research, or experimental development—and explicitly included, under paragraph 2900(1)(d), work with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, and testing, provided such work was commensurate with the needs and directly in support of the core research or development activities.
The Court's Final Holding

Judge Bowman dismissed LGL Limited's substantive claim regarding the foreign field expenditures, holding that physical data collection performed outside Canada, even when scientifically indispensable to a Canadian SR&ED project, constitutes SR&ED "carried on outside Canada" under subsection 37(2) rather than SR&ED "carried on in Canada" under paragraph 37(1)(a). In articulating this ruling, Bowman T.C.J. did not overrule or expressly decline to follow the two recent Tax Court of Canada precedents relied on by the appellant—Tigney Technology Inc. v. R., [1997] 2 C.T.C. 2333 (T.C.C.) and Data Kinetics Ltd. v. R. (1998), 98 D.T.C. 1877 (T.C.C.)—in which costs of activities conducted outside Canada had been held to qualify. Because Tigney Technology was under appeal to the Federal Court of Appeal, he made no comment on it beyond observing that the Kentucky experiments there appeared to have been a rather small incident of the SR&ED carried on in Canada, whereas the very basis of LGL Limited's SR&ED was the data collected off the shore of Alaska; and he distinguished Data Kinetics on the basis that no personnel of that taxpayer ever went to the U.S. and that, on the facts found in that case, the entire project was carried on in Canada. It was the Federal Court of Appeal that later stated it could not agree with either decision. The appeals for the 1992 and 1993 taxation years were dismissed in their entirety, and the appeal for the 1991 taxation year was allowed solely to give effect to the partial consent to judgment regarding the Snow Goose and Eider projects. LGL Limited subsequently appealed to the Federal Court of Appeal (Docket A-139-99), which heard the matter in tandem with the Crown's appeal in Tigney Technology Inc. On February 7, 2000, the Federal Court of Appeal (Robertson, Rothstein, and McDonald JJ.A.) unanimously dismissed LGL Limited's appeal with costs (reported at 2000 D.T.C. 6108 (F.C.A.)), fully endorsing Bowman T.C.J.'s statutory interpretation and cementing the territorial severance rule in Canadian tax jurisprudence.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures
The Fallacy of the Monolithic Project Doctrine

The primary legal deficiency in LGL Limited's position stemmed from its reliance on a monolithic "project-as-a-whole" theory that conflated the qualitative definition of SR&ED under Regulation 2900 with the territorial allocation rules of subsections 37(1) and 37(2). At trial, Judge Bowman accepted, at paragraph 44 of the reasons for judgment, four factual conclusions upon which the appellant relied: first, that the field work involving the collection of biological data had to be done outside Canada and could not physically have been done in Canada; second, that the data-collection work done outside Canada, standing by itself, was not SR&ED, and only became SR&ED when it was assimilated into and made part of the overall SR&ED project; third, that the assembly of this field data was an essential and necessary part of the overall projects; and fourth, that if it were relevant to designate the projects, looked at in their entirety, as Canadian or non-Canadian, it would be more accurate to describe them as Canadian, because the work was done by a Canadian company using Canadian researchers and personnel, and all the core scientific work was done in Canada.

Armed with these factual concessions, the appellant invoked Tigney Technology Inc. v. R. and Data Kinetics Ltd. v. R., arguing that an SR&ED project is an organic, indivisible whole that cannot be carved up into constituent geographic tasks. Under the appellant's interpretation, because the intellectual direction, experimental hypothesis formulation, data assimilation, and scientific conclusions occurred in LGL Limited's Canadian facilities in Ontario, British Columbia, and Newfoundland, the entire project was "carried on in Canada". Judge Bowman rejected this position, stating that he could see no particular reason for the appellant's conclusion either as a matter of principle or as a matter of statutory interpretation, and observing that a project-as-a-whole approach would cut both ways: if an overall project were held to be essentially non-Canadian because a predominant part of the activity was carried on outside Canada, the cost of activities actually carried on in Canada could be denied paragraph 37(1)(a) treatment. The Court held that the words "carried on in Canada" in paragraph 37(1)(a) are reasonably clear and comprehensible, and that where part of an SR&ED project is carried on in Canada and part elsewhere, the costs can be split on a reasonable basis between the two according to where the work is in fact carried on, not according to the jurisdiction where the overarching project is conceived or where the resulting data is eventually synthesized.
The Standalone Support Work Characterization Trap

A closely related issue concerned the reasoning in a decision on which LGL Limited relied, namely the "statutory vacuum" paradox formulated by the Tax Court in Data Kinetics Ltd. v. R.. In Data Kinetics, the trial judge had posited that if a single SR&ED project were subdivided into domestic development and foreign testing/data collection, each severed component would have to be evaluated independently against the criteria of Regulation 2900. Following that premise, the Data Kinetics court observed that when component parts "considered alone fail to meet the requirements of Regulation 2900, then neither of subsections 37(1) or (2) would apply as the activities would not constitute SR&ED". LGL Limited's position, as summarized by the Court at paragraph 47, was that because its foreign field data collection was not SR&ED by itself and only became SR&ED through its integration into the project as a whole (the factual conclusion the Court accepted at paragraph 44(b)), that work had to form part of an SR&ED project carried on in Canada. Simply put, the appellant contended that a project qualifying as SR&ED must be looked at integrally and a determination made as to whether, as a whole, it is carried on in Canada or outside Canada; the reasons do not record any argument by the appellant that severance would bar the foreign costs from deduction under subsection 37(2).

Judge Bowman did not expressly address this paradox—he distinguished Data Kinetics on its facts—but his reasoning rested on a two-stage sequence for interpreting the Act and Regulations (a sequence the appellant's own counsel recognized in written argument), which the Federal Court of Appeal later relied on to hold the concern unfounded. At Stage One, the adjudicator evaluates the project as a whole under Regulation 2900 to determine whether the overarching investigation constitutes eligible SR&ED. During this initial threshold stage, commensurate support activities listed in paragraph 2900(1)(d)—such as LGL Limited's field data collection—are assimilated into the core research project and thereby acquire the legal status of SR&ED. Once the entire project (including its assimilated support activities) is stamped with the character of SR&ED under Regulation 2900, the inquiry moves to Stage Two: allocating the now-qualified SR&ED expenditures between subsection 37(1) and subsection 37(2) based strictly on whether the physical work was carried on inside or outside Canada. Because the Regulation 2900 determination occurs prior to the geographic allocation under section 37, the foreign data collection retains its derivative SR&ED status when allocated to subsection 37(2); on appeal, the Federal Court of Appeal expressly relied on this sequence in holding that the statutory vacuum concern expressed in Data Kinetics was unfounded.
Insufficiency of the Physical and Environmental Necessity Doctrine

From a technical and evidentiary standpoint, LGL Limited placed heavy emphasis on proving that its foreign expenditures were not discretionary outsourcing decisions, but immutable scientific necessities dictated by nature. The appellant adduced evidence—substantially through a detailed partial agreed statement of facts, supplemented by the expert report of zoologist Dr. Roger H. Green (accepted by the respondent without cross-examination) and the viva voce testimony of its president, Dr. Rolph A. Davis—demonstrating that the field data for each project could only be obtained in or off northern Alaska: the whales could safely be observed only off Point Barrow, the Oldsquaw study required comparable disturbed and undisturbed moulting areas with nine years of background survey data, the Eider study depended on solid-fill oil-industry causeways that do not exist in the Canadian Arctic, and the fish study concerned the Endicott causeway itself. While Judge Bowman accepted this evidence unequivocally at paragraph 44(a)—finding that the collection of data had to be done outside Canada and could not have been done within Canada—the Court held that such necessity did not change where the work was in fact carried on, and therefore did not bring the outside-Canada work within the words "carried on in Canada" in paragraph 37(1)(a) as they applied in the 1991, 1992, and 1993 taxation years.

The taxpayer's failure lay in assuming that the purposive spirit of the SR&ED incentive regime allowed the Court to read an implied "nexus of necessity" exception into the plain words "carried on in Canada". Judge Bowman described as unassailable the appellant's own written submission that subsections 37(1) and 37(2) are drafted to be mutually exclusive, so that whether activities constitute SR&ED must be determined before deciding whether that SR&ED is carried on in or outside Canada. Where Parliament has explicitly enacted a specific statutory provision (subsection 37(2)) to govern the tax treatment of SR&ED conducted outside Canada, a taxpayer cannot bypass that provision and claim the richer fiscal incentives of subsection 37(1) merely by proving that Canadian geography lacked the environmental conditions required for the experiment.
Cross-Border Affiliate Governance and Project Ownership Ambiguities

Beyond the geographic severance issue, the procedural history of LGL Ltd. v. R. also touched on project attribution between the Canadian appellant and a cross-border affiliate. LGL Limited was affiliated with two research companies, in Texas and Alaska, and the partial consent to judgment shows that whether the Snow Goose Project and the Eider Project were projects of LGL Limited or of LGL Alaska had been in issue; the Court found it unnecessary to set out the detailed terms of the consent, and the reasons do not describe the documentation presented on audit. Under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) and subsection 37(2), an expenditure is only eligible if the research is "directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer, and related to a business of the taxpayer".

When a Canadian company utilizes a foreign subsidiary or shares scientific personnel across borders without air-tight intercompany research agreements, clear intellectual property vesting clauses, and segregated project accounting, the Minister will routinely challenge whether the SR&ED is actually being undertaken by and for the business of the foreign affiliate rather than on behalf of the Canadian claimant. Although LGL Limited ultimately succeeded in securing a partial consent to judgment confirming that the Snow Goose and Eider projects were projects of the appellant and not of LGL Alaska, the fact that this attribution question was in issue before the Tax Court underscores the audit risk that can arise when project ownership between a Canadian claimant and a foreign affiliate is contested, although the reasons do not identify what gave rise to the dispute.
Financial Tracking and Overhead Allocation Contamination

The evidentiary record reproduced in Judge Bowman's decision—specifically the schedule titled "LGL LIMITED'S TOTALS OF TIME AND MONEY SPENT (including allocation of overhead) Inside and Outside Canada on the Projects in Issue"—illustrates the financial stakes of the foreign portion of the projects, although Judge Bowman cautioned that these figures must be used with caution and that no reliable conclusion can be reached by totalling up dollars and days and arriving at unweighted percentages. Charts in evidence set out, project by project, the time and money spent inside Canada and outside Canada, and the appellant's allowable overhead allocable to SR&ED was determined under a formula the parties agreed was acceptable (fees billed on SR&ED projects multiplied by the ratio of the appellant's total overhead to its total fees), so that a reduction of fees billed on SR&ED projects reduced the overhead allocable to SR&ED.

Because the costs had in fact already been split between the work done in Canada and the work done outside Canada (as Judge Bowman noted at paragraph 58), two compounding tax consequences followed once the Court upheld the denial of paragraph 37(1)(a) treatment for the outside-Canada work. First, the direct costs of the work done outside Canada were denied paragraph 37(1)(a) treatment and, with it, eligibility for the refundable ITC. Second, because the appellant's overhead allocable to SR&ED was computed by reference to fees billed on SR&ED projects, the portion of overhead allocable to the outside-Canada work was likewise excluded from the paragraph 37(1)(a) claim. Furthermore, any scientific analysis, hypothesis refinement, or experimental design work that a researcher may have performed prior to departure or immediately upon return, if lumped into a generalized "field campaign" cost center without granular daily activity logs distinguishing domestic analytical hours from foreign data-gathering hours, risked being swept into the foreign disallowance percentage.

cells: Holistic Project Qualification as SR&ED
Subsection 37(7) [now s. 248(1)] and Regulation 2900(1)(a)–(c)
Asserted that each environmental research project (studying industrial impacts on whales, birds, and fish) constituted an integrated, systematic scientific investigation.
Satisfied (Admitted by Crown): The determination of whether a project is SR&ED under Regulation 2900 is made at the initial threshold stage by evaluating the project as a whole.
Eligibility of Commensurate Support Work (Data Collection)
Regulation 2900(1)(d)

Contended that because field data collection outside Canada was not SR&ED on its own and only became SR&ED through integration into the overall project, it had to form part of an SR&ED project carried on in Canada (para. 47), relying on Tigney Technology and Data Kinetics.

Rejected Severance Immunity: Support work acquires SR&ED status at Stage One by assimilation into the overall project under Reg. 2900; it retains that SR&ED character when subsequently allocated geographically at Stage Two.
Territorial Locus: "Carried on in Canada"
Paragraph 37(1)(a) of the Income Tax Act
Argued that because the project was directed, analyzed, and synthesized in Canadian labs (King City, Sidney, St. John's), the entire project was "carried on in Canada" per Tigney Technology.
Failed Strict Physical Locus Test: "Carried on in Canada" requires the physical performance of the activity within Canadian geographic borders; foreign field work is excluded from s. 37(1)(a).
Geographic / Environmental Necessity Exception
Paragraph 37(1)(a) vs. Subsection 37(2) of the Income Tax Act

Demonstrated that the field data for each project could only be collected in or off northern Alaska (the only safe whale-observation site off Point Barrow; Alaskan disturbed and control moulting areas with nine years of background data; oil-industry causeways absent from the Canadian Arctic), so the work could not have been done in Canada.

Legally Irrelevant under s. 37(1)(a): Even where foreign execution is an absolute scientific necessity (Finding 44(a)), the Act contains no necessity exception to convert s. 37(2) work into s. 37(1) work.
Treatment of SR&ED "Carried on Outside Canada"
Subsection 37(2) of the Income Tax Act
Argued that s. 37(2) only applies to self-contained foreign SR&ED projects, not to subordinate data-collection tasks supporting a Canadian project.
Applied to Severed Foreign Tasks: Subsections 37(1) and 37(2) are mutually exclusive territorial buckets; all foreign field data-collection expenditures fall solely under s. 37(2).
Investment Tax Credit (ITC) & Overhead Allocation
Subsections 37(1), 37(2), and 127(9) of the Income Tax Act
Claimed refundable ITCs and allocated corporate overhead across total project time and money spent both inside and outside Canada.

Disallowed for Foreign Portion: Expenditures governed by s. 37(2) do not give rise to ITCs, and the portion of overhead allocable to the outside-Canada work (computed under the agreed fees-billed formula) likewise falls outside the s. 37(1)(a) claim; only the costs of work carried on in Canada qualify.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To assist Canadian corporations and technical tax advisors in navigating the structural hazards exposed in LGL Ltd. v. R., the following two industry case studies demonstrate how projects facing identical cross-border data-collection, affiliate-attribution, and overhead-contamination challenges must be engineered and documented. In applying these remedial strategies, advisors must also account for Parliament's subsequent legislative enactment (for expenditures made after February 25, 2008) of subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) of the Income Tax Act (which permit a limited carve-out for salaries and wages of Canadian-resident employees for SR&ED carried on outside Canada that is directly undertaken by the taxpayer and solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada, up to a strict cap of 10% of the taxpayer's salary or wages for SR&ED carried on in Canada), while recognizing that the LGL Ltd. territorial severance principle remains completely fatal to all foreign contractor outlays, foreign travel and supply expenses, non-resident affiliate labour, and any foreign employee wages exceeding the statutory threshold.
Case Study 1: Marine Autonomous Hydroacoustic Telemetry & Cetacean Tracking (Oceanographic & Environmental Engineering Sector)
Project Scenario and Inherent LGL Ltd. Pitfalls

Pacifica Marine Telemetry Inc. ("Pacifica"), a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) headquartered in Sidney, British Columbia, with a computational acoustics laboratory in St. John's, Newfoundland, is developing a real-time, edge-computed passive acoustic monitoring (PAM) system mounted on autonomous underwater gliders. The technological objective is to overcome signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) degradation caused by industrial seismic reflection arrays and Arctic pack-ice cracking, enabling automated taxonomic classification of vocalizing bowhead and fin whales in high-noise marine environments. Because the specific acoustic interference profile of multi-streamer seismic vessels interacting with shallow-water bowhead whale aggregations only occurs during summer open-water seasons in the Beaufort and Chukchi Seas off the coast of Alaska, Pacifica deploys a field team—assisted by its wholly owned U.S. subsidiary, Pacifica Alaska LLC—for 45 days in Alaskan waters to deploy the gliders and record raw acoustic arrays.

If structured naively in the manner of LGL Ltd. v. R., Pacifica faces three severe audit disqualifications: first, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) will sever the entire 45-day Alaskan field campaign under subsection 37(2), disallowing all foreign glider charter vessels, travel costs, and U.S. subcontractor fees from earning the 35% refundable CCPC Investment Tax Credit; second, because Pacifica uses a single global project code for "Bowhead Acoustic Project," its domestic proxy overhead calculation (the 55% prescribed proxy election under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)) and domestic engineering time during the summer window risk downward adjustment due to blended tracking; and third, because Pacifica Alaska LLC obtained the U.S. marine mammal research permits in its own name, the CRA may assert—just as the question whether the Snow Goose and Eider projects were projects of the Canadian appellant or of LGL Alaska was in issue in LGL Ltd.—that the research is actually the project of the U.S. subsidiary rather than the Canadian parent.
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and Sub-Project Partitioning

To insulate the Canadian SR&ED claim from geographic contamination, Pacifica must abandon monolithic project accounting and partition the initiative into distinct technical work packages that separate core domestic experimental development from foreign field data acquisition. Work Package A (Domestic Experimental Development & Simulation) must be anchored entirely in the Sidney and St. John's laboratories. Rather than waiting to perform algorithm iteration aboard vessels in Alaskan waters, Pacifica's engineers must construct a synthetic hydroacoustic testbed in Canada using historical acoustic datasets and anechoic water-tank transducers to execute the iterative hypothesis testing inside Canada. Work Package B (Foreign Field Data Acquisition & Validation) is strictly ring-fenced to cover only the physical deployment, recovery, and raw recording activities in Alaskan waters. By compressing the physical presence in Alaska strictly to raw data capture—and transmitting the raw acoustic packets daily via satellite link back to the Sidney, B.C. laboratory where Canadian-based acousticians perform the real-time signal analysis, parameter tuning, and firmware recompilation—Pacifica converts what would have been 45 days of foreign engineering labour into 45 days of domestic SR&ED analysis "carried on in Canada" under paragraph 37(1)(a), leaving only a minimal 5-day physical launch-and-recovery technician deployment outside Canada.
Step 2: Technical Documentation and Technological Uncertainty Framing

In LGL Ltd. v. R., the taxpayer framed its claim around the environmental study as an ecological whole, which highlighted the centrality of the foreign wildlife observations. Pacifica must restructure its technical narratives (Form T661 Part 2) to define the technological uncertainty strictly in terms of acoustic signal processing physics and embedded hardware architecture rather than biological population surveys. The documentation must articulate the system-level uncertainty: whether a convolutional neural network quantized to run on a low-power 1.5-watt ARM microcontroller inside a glider pressure hull can distinguish non-stationary bowhead whale frequency-modulated calls from multipath seismic airgun reverberations below a 3 dB SNR threshold. By framing the core experimental loop around the mathematical modeling and algorithmic architecture executed in British Columbia and Newfoundland, the Alaskan field data is properly contextualized under Regulation 2900(1)(d) (now statutory definition subsection 248(1) paragraph (d)) as boundary-condition verification data supporting a squarely Canadian experimental development project.
Step 3: Contractual Terms and Intercompany Structuring

To neutralize the LGL Alaska entity-attribution hazard that jeopardized the Snow Goose and Eider projects in LGL Ltd. v. R., Pacifica must execute a formal, contemporaneous Master Intercompany Research Services and Permit Agency Agreement with Pacifica Alaska LLC prior to the commencement of the taxation year. This agreement must establish clear agency status for regulatory permits, stipulating that Pacifica Alaska LLC holds all U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM) marine research permits strictly as a bare nominee and administrative agent on behalf of Pacifica (Canada). Furthermore, the contract must mandate exclusive intellectual property vesting and economic risk allocation, confirming that all raw hydroacoustic datasets, telemetry logs, firmware modifications, and intellectual property generated during the Alaskan deployment vest ab initio and exclusively in Pacifica (Canada), which bears 100% of the financial and technical risk of failure. The scope of the subsidiary's mandate must be contractually restricted to providing logistical vessel support and marine launch assistance on a fee-for-service basis, with zero authority to direct scientific hypotheses or modify experimental protocols. Finally, the agreement must enforce strict invoicing and cost segregation, requiring all intercompany charges from Pacifica Alaska LLC to be billed under a separate non-SR&ED or subsection 37(2) general ledger account so that non-qualifying foreign affiliate payments never contaminate the subsection 37(1) Canadian expenditure pool.
Step 4: Experimentation and Financial/Time Tracking Protocols

To overcome the evidentiary weaknesses seen in LGL Limited's aggregate time-and-money schedules, Pacifica must implement a dual-attribute time-tracking ledger that records both the Regulation 2900 / s. 248(1) Activity Code and the Physical GPS / Geolocation Locus of every employee on an hourly basis. When two Canadian-resident marine technicians travel to Alaska for the 5-day launch and recovery window, their time logs must record the exact date and hour of border crossing. Because these two technicians are Canadian residents on Pacifica's Canadian payroll (T4), and because the statutory conditions of subsection 37(1.4) (which are distinct from, and not derived from, the factual conclusions accepted at paragraph 44 of LGL Ltd.) are met—namely, that the work is SR&ED carried on outside Canada, directly undertaken by Pacifica, related to its business, performed by employees resident in Canada, and solely in support of Pacifica's SR&ED carried on in Canada (a record strengthened by documenting that the Arctic acoustic data collection cannot physically be performed in Canadian waters due to the specific seismic-whale overlap)—Pacifica can isolate their 5-day salary cost into the dedicated subsection 37(1.4) sub-ledger (capped at 10% of the T4 SR&ED salary base carried on in Canada). All charter vessel fees, airfare, Alaskan lodging, and payments to Pacifica Alaska LLC are routed directly to a separate subsection 37(2) current deduction ledger, preserving 100% of the refundable ITCs and proxy overhead allocations on the remaining 98% of the project's engineering hours performed in Sidney and St. John's.
Case Study 2: Airborne Millimetre-Wave Avian-Strike Avoidance Radar Systems (Aerospace & Avionics Sector)
Project Scenario and Inherent LGL Ltd. Pitfalls

AeroShield Avionics Corp. ("AeroShield"), an aerospace engineering firm based in King City, Ontario, is developing an active electronically scanned array (AESA) W-band millimetre-wave radar and micro-Doppler wing-beat classification processor designed to detect flocking birds in real time during aircraft takeoff and landing, directly addressing the "bird hazards to aircraft" research domain highlighted in LGL Ltd. v. R.. The technological uncertainty centres on eliminating ground-clutter backscattering and atmospheric attenuation caused by heavy tropical convective rain while accurately resolving the non-rigid micro-Doppler radar cross-section (RCS) of large-bodied flocking waterbirds. During the Canadian winter (November to March), high-density congregations of target avian species combined with severe tropical convective precipitation do not exist in Canadian airspace. Consequently, AeroShield dispatches a flight-test engineering crew and a leased twin-turboprop testbed aircraft to a flight facility in southern Florida and Panama for 60 days to conduct airborne radar sweeps and collect raw I/Q (in-phase and quadrature) radar return data.

Under the LGL Ltd. v. R. precedent, AeroShield's traditional method of accounting for the 60-day southern flight campaign as an indivisible phase of its King City engineering project will fail upon CRA technical and financial review. Even though testing the radar against live tropical rain clutter and winter migratory flocks cannot physically be accomplished in Ontario during January (satisfying Finding 44(a) of LGL Ltd.), and even though raw radar data collection alone is not standalone SR&ED until assimilated into the King City signal-processing development (Finding 44(b)), the Tax Court's two-stage statutory rule dictates that the 60 days of flight testing are "carried on outside Canada" under subsection 37(2). As a result, all aircraft fuel, foreign hangar leases, third-party pilot contractors, and foreign engineering time exceeding statutory limits will be stripped of ITCs and overhead allocations.
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and Sub-Project Partitioning

To prevent the wholesale reclassification of its winter engineering quarter into subsection 37(2), AeroShield must fundamentally re-architect where and how its experimental iterations occur. Instead of deploying six senior radar systems engineers to Florida for 60 days to modify waveform chirp parameters and debug FPGA signal-processing code at the foreign airfield, AeroShield must restrict the foreign flight crew to a third-party commercial flight contractor or a two-person technician crew operating a pre-programmed, automated data-logging pod mounted on the aircraft.

Simultaneously, AeroShield must establish a domestic hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) RF waveform injection simulator at its King City, Ontario laboratory. At the end of each 3-hour flight sortie in Florida, the raw multi-terabyte I/Q radar return files are uploaded via high-speed fiber link to the King City laboratory. The six senior radar engineers remain physically in Ontario, injecting the captured tropical clutter and avian micro-Doppler signatures into the domestic HIL radar processor, formulating hypotheses regarding clutter-suppression filter coefficients, re-synthesizing the VHDL/Verilog gateware in King City, and transmitting updated radar waveform configuration files back to the aircraft for the next day's sortie. Through this operational restructuring, the core systematic investigation by means of experiment or analysis (Regulation 2900(1) / s. 248(1)) is physically performed in Ontario, reducing the foreign activity to a bare minimum of automated sensor transport.
Step 2: Technical Documentation and Technological Uncertainty Framing

In preparing its contemporaneous technical documentation, AeroShield must avoid describing the foreign flight campaign as "Field Experimental Development Phase 2". In LGL Ltd. v. R., the costs of the work done outside Canada had in fact been split from those of the work done in Canada, and Judge Bowman cautioned that totals of days and dollars, particularly unweighted percentages across projects, could be misleading and result in distorted or erroneous conclusions. Instead, AeroShield's project documentation must strictly bifurcate the domestic experimental development loops from the foreign environmental data-capture runs. Each experimental iteration in the King City laboratory must be logged in a structured hypothesis-test-analysis registry that begins by recording the domestic technological hypothesis formulated in King City regarding specific adaptive Kalman filtering and Space-Time Adaptive Processing (STAP) matrices designed to suppress convective rain backscatter at 94 GHz. Next, the registry must document the domestic HIL experimentation, capturing the execution of the modified STAP algorithm on the King City RF hardware emulator using previously captured boundary-condition datasets. Finally, the registry must link each domestic test to a commensurate data-collection specification—a formal engineering requisition issued from King City specifying the exact flight altitudes, radar grazing angles, and pulse-repetition frequencies required from the foreign flight pod solely to acquire new raw verification datasets under paragraph 2900(1)(d).
Step 3: Contractual Terms and Third-Party Subcontracting

If AeroShield contracts a Canadian aviation services company (e.g., an Ottawa-based special-mission flight operator) to fly the radar pod to Florida and collect the data, a critical legal trap arises under paragraph 37(1)(a). Many taxpayers mistakenly believe that paying a Canadian subcontractor in Canadian dollars under a domestic contract automatically qualifies the payment as SR&ED "carried on in Canada". Under the territorial principle of LGL Ltd. v. R., the physical location where the subcontractor's personnel actually perform the work governs eligibility under section 37, regardless of the subcontractor's corporate residency.

Consequently, AeroShield must structure its Special Mission Flight Services Contract with the Canadian aviation provider using an explicit Schedule of Territorial Cost Unbundling. The contract must legally obligate the aviation subcontractor to invoice domestic engineering, mechanical integration, airworthiness certification, and Canadian test flights (performed in Ontario airspace to calibrate the radar pod prior to departure) under Contract Line Item 001 (Domestic Canadian Execution), and to separately invoice the transit and southern data-collection flight hours performed in U.S./Panamanian airspace under Contract Line Item 002 (Foreign Airspace Execution). By contractually mandating itemized territorial billing, AeroShield preserves full subsection 37(1)(a) eligibility and ITC recovery on the costly domestic airframe integration and Canadian calibration flights, while cleanly isolating the foreign flight hours into subsection 37(2) so that the CRA cannot taint or disallow the entire subcontract for lack of geographic breakdown.
Step 4: Experimentation and Financial/Time Tracking Protocols
To achieve audit-proof financial compliance that satisfies the Tax Court's evidentiary standards, AeroShield must implement a three-tier general ledger and time-tracking architecture:

cells: Tier 1: Domestic Core R&D & HIL Analysis
Logged via biometric/VPN-verified daily timesheets in King City, Ontario, mapped to specific STAP algorithm and FPGA hardware iterations.
Paragraph 37(1)(a): 100% eligible for SR&ED pool, full 55% prescribed proxy overhead allocation, and full refundable/non-refundable ITCs.
Tier 2: Canadian-Resident Technician Foreign Deployment

Strictly limited to one T4 Canadian-resident radar technician accompanying the aircraft for 10 days of sensor calibration outside Canada; logged with border-crossing timestamps and environmental necessity justification (Finding 44(a)).
Subsection 37(1.4) Carve-Out: Eligible for s. 37(1) treatment and ITCs up to the statutory cap of 10% of Tier 1 Canadian direct SR&ED labour; zero foreign overhead contamination.
Tier 3: Foreign Flight Operations, Travel & Excess Labour

Isolated into a dedicated Foreign Support GL Code covering Contract Line Item 002 (foreign flight hours), aviation fuel outside Canada, foreign hangar fees, travel expenses, and any foreign hours exceeding the 10% cap.

Subsection 37(2): Fully deductible as a current business expense in computing net income for the year under s. 37(2), cleanly excluded from Form T661 ITC claims to prevent audit reassessment and penalties.

body.text: By implementing this four-step remedial framework across project governance, technical documentation, contractual unbundling, and granular accounting, Canadian taxpayers can fully internalize the statutory lessons of LGL Ltd. v. R., maximizing domestic SR&ED Investment Tax Credits and overhead recovery while neutralizing the territorial severance risks inherent in cross-border scientific operations.
